prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, February, Undivided

outputs.L1:
The deer, racing across a field  
of the same clay-and-tallow color they are—  
if they are: or are they tricks of the light?—  
must feel themselves being poured  
and pouring through life. We are not built  
but become: trembling columns  
of apprehension that ripple  
and pass those ripples to and fro  
with the world that shakes around us—  
it, too, is something poured  
and ceaselessly pouring itself.  
February shakes the fields  
and trembles in each yellow willow.  

•  

The violin’s back is not veneer—  
the strummed wood shudders together.  
Undivided by caution,  
each note is its own first thought.  
My first thought is a kind of prayer:  
that I might resonate entire—  
sometimes it is such a meager portion  
shaking a little, as if it ought...  
Every day, the same desire  
to push myself through the door  
that leads to some bright place,  
brighter than the concert platform,  
where the whole self echoes together—  
the outer to the inner pleasure.  

•  

Everything runs together—  
the light smells of spring,  
the unreasonable brightness  
of this peg, this sheet, this line tethering  
linen between sky and mud,  
as if the garden marked a pause  
in that eternal return  
whose looping trace is the blood  
hissing through the ventricles.  
What gives you life is the thing that kills.
outputs.L2:
Deer sprint over a field  
the very color of themselves—clay mixed with tallow—  
if they are really there at all,  
and not only a flicker the light invents.  
They must sense their bodies as something flowing,  
as though life were being poured through them  
and they were pouring with it.  

We are not manufactured whole;  
we come into being instead—  
quivering pillars of fear and awareness,  
sending our tremors outward and receiving them back  
from the shaken world around us,  
a world also spilling forward,  
endlessly emptying and refilling itself.  
February rattles the fields  
and shivers inside every yellow willow.  

•  

The violin’s back is no thin facing;  
when it is played, the wood vibrates as one.  
Free of division, free of restraint,  
each sound arrives like an original impulse.  
My own first impulse is almost a prayer:  
let me sound through completely.  
Yet sometimes only a small part of me  
quakes faintly, as though it should do more.  

Each day I want the same thing:  
to force myself through the doorway  
into some radiant elsewhere,  
brighter even than the stage where music is performed,  
a place where the entire self resounds at once,  
where outward sensation answers inward joy.  

•  

All things blur into one another—  
the light carries the scent of spring,  
and this clothespin, this sheet, this line  
stretching linen between sky and mud  
shine with an irrational brilliance,  
as if the garden had placed a brief rest  
inside that everlasting recurrence  
whose circling mark is the blood  
whispering through the heart’s chambers.  

The source of your living  
is also what brings your death.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents life as a continuous process of becoming. Nothing in it appears fixed or complete; instead, beings and the world seem to tremble, flow, and reshape one another. Life is shown as movement rather than stability, as a constant exchange between the self and its surroundings. The natural world is not a static background but an active, shifting presence that participates in the speaker’s emotional and imaginative experience.

Images such as the deer, the fields, the willows, and the February weather all suggest a nature that is unstable and fluid. These details blur the boundary between what is actually seen and what is felt or imagined. The deer may appear almost dreamlike, the fields seem to change with light and weather, and the willows evoke softness, bending, and motion. February itself is a transitional month, caught between winter and spring, death and renewal. Through these images, the poem suggests that nature cannot be easily separated from perception or illusion. The world is real, but it is also shaped by the mind that encounters it.

The violin’s resonant wood becomes an important metaphor for the desire to feel whole, undivided, and fully alive. A violin produces music because its body vibrates; its wood must resonate in order to give voice to sound. In the same way, the speaker longs for a state of being in which the body, mind, and spirit can vibrate together without separation. The instrument represents an ideal of harmony, where inner feeling and outward expression become one continuous music.

This longing leads the speaker toward the desire to pass into a brighter, more intense state of existence. The poem imagines a condition in which the inner self and the outer world can echo one another perfectly. Such harmony would allow the speaker to feel not fragmented or divided, but fully present and alive. Brightness, resonance, and movement all become signs of this hoped-for transformation.

At the same time, the poem does not treat beauty and renewal as separate from mortality. The vitality of nature is closely connected to decay, change, and death. February’s promise of spring still carries the memory of winter, and the living world is sustained by processes that also involve loss. The poem therefore suggests that what gives life its beauty and energy is also what binds it to death. Renewal is possible only because things pass away, and vitality is meaningful because it is temporary. In this way, the poem presents existence as both fragile and radiant, shaped by the inseparable forces of life, change, and mortality.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the fluid, trembling nature of life and selfhood through a series of delicate, shifting images: deer moving through open fields, the cold bareness of February, music passing through the air, light touching the world, and blood circulating within the body. These images do not remain separate. Instead, they echo one another, suggesting that life is not fixed or solid but constantly in motion, vibrating between visibility and disappearance, presence and absence, vitality and fragility.

The deer represent a kind of alert, instinctive life. They appear as creatures both physical and elusive, fully alive yet difficult to hold in thought for long. Their movement through the February fields evokes a landscape that is sparse, transitional, and exposed. February is neither the depth of winter nor the fullness of spring; it is a threshold month, marked by cold but also by the first suggestion of renewal. In this setting, life seems tentative and vulnerable, but also persistent. The deer’s bodies become signs of survival, grace, and nervous energy within a world that is still half-frozen.

Music and light deepen this sense of resonance. Music moves invisibly, felt more than seen, while light reveals and transforms whatever it touches. Together, they suggest that existence is made of vibrations, perceptions, and fleeting intensities. The self in the poem is not isolated from the world but continually shaped by it. What happens outside the body—the motion of animals, the season, the changing light—finds an answering movement inside the speaker. Likewise, what happens within the body—pulse, breath, circulation, emotion—seems connected to the larger rhythms of nature.

The image of bodily circulation is especially important because it brings the poem’s reflections back to the living body. Blood moving through the veins becomes a physical version of the poem’s larger pattern of flow and exchange. Life is carried through the body just as sound is carried through air and light across a field. Yet this same circulation also reminds us of mortality. The force that keeps the body alive is inseparable from the fact that the body is temporary. To feel life moving inside oneself is also to sense how fragile that life is.

In this way, the poem presents existence as a continuous resonance between inner and outer worlds. The boundary between the self and its surroundings becomes porous: the field enters the mind, music enters the body, light becomes feeling, and the movement of deer mirrors the tremor of human awareness. The poem suggests that to be alive is to participate in a larger current of energy, one that passes through animals, landscapes, bodies, and sounds. This current animates all living things, but it also carries them toward disappearance. Life and mortality are therefore not opposites in the poem; they are intertwined aspects of the same force.

Ultimately, the poem finds beauty in this fragile continuity. It does not present selfhood as something stable or separate, but as something responsive, trembling, and alive because it is constantly touched by the world. The poem’s images create a vision of life as both luminous and vulnerable, filled with motion yet shadowed by loss. Existence becomes a kind of music: temporary, embodied, and resonant, fading even as it sounds.
outputs.L5:
The February sky was pale and quiet, stretching above the town like a soft blanket of winter light. Snow rested on rooftops, and the streets seemed to move more slowly than usual, as if the whole world had paused to listen.

In that stillness, the community felt undivided. Neighbors greeted one another warmly, children shared laughter in the cold air, and families gathered close as the short days passed. Though February often brought frost and gray mornings, it also reminded everyone of the strength found in unity.

The season was not only about winter’s chill, but about togetherness—an undivided spirit that carried people toward the promise of spring.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary lyric poem in three sections separated by bullets, meditating on deer in a February field, a violin resonating, and spring laundry on a line; use dense enjambment and philosophical imagery about becoming, vibration, and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
The deer stand where the field  
has not yet decided whether to be snow  
or memory of snow, February thinning  
its white breath over the stubble—  
their bodies are questions made of hunger,  
brown parentheses around the bare trees,  
and each raised head seems to listen  
past us, past the road’s salt-bleached shoulder,  
into the unfinished grammar of thaw.  
What is becoming but this:  
a hoof sinking, then lifting,  
the earth accepting the print  
as if it were a name it must forget.  
They move without doctrine,  
muscle and alertness braided  
to the brief republic of the pulse,  
while the sky lowers its gray bowl  
over everything mortal enough  
to need shelter, everything alive  
because it can be startled.

•

Inside, the violin waits against a chair,  
wood shaped into a chamber  
for vanishing—maple, spruce, glue,  
the animal hair of the bow drawn  
across a string until air itself  
is persuaded into grief.  
A note begins as pressure,  
becomes tremor, becomes room,  
enters the sternum and finds there  
another string, older, untuned,  
still willing to answer.  
Is the self anything more  
than resonance, a body’s temporary  
agreement with motion,  
a held frequency before the hand  
lifts and the sound goes on  
without us, thinner, elsewhere?  
The deer would hear it differently,  
not as music but as weather  
inside the walls, a branch  
of invisible lightning,  
the world remembering  
it was once all vibration  
and will be again—ash, dust,  
the last note loosening  
from the instrument of bone.

•

By April the laundry is out,  
shirts and sheets clipped to the line  
like flags of surrender  
to the ordinary wind.  
They fill, collapse, fill again,  
white lungs practicing  
for some larger breathing,  
and sunlight moves through them  
with such clean indifference  
it almost feels like mercy.  
After the deer, after the dark  
varnished hollow of the violin,  
after all our thinking has failed  
to keep anything from passing,  
here is cotton becoming weather,  
water becoming shine,  
the body’s odors lifted  
into blue, into nothing  
we can own.  
The sleeves wave without arms.  
The sheets billow, then fall back,  
as if death were not an ending  
but a change in how the invisible  
touches us—  
as if every life, rinsed and wrung,  
were hung for a little while  
between earth and sky,  
bright with use,  
trembling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem in the style of a modern nature poet, with images of clay-colored deer, yellow willow, a violin’s wooden back, and a clothesline between sky and mud, ending on the idea that what gives life also kills.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk the deer come down,  
clay-colored,  
as if the hillside shaped them wet  
and set them moving.

Yellow willow loosens its hair  
over the ditch,  
each leaf a small flame  
learning the patience of water.

In the house, a violin rests  
on its wooden back,  
dark as a pond under trees,  
holding in its curved ribs  
the old weather of a forest.

Outside, the clothesline  
hangs between sky and mud—  
shirts swelling with wind,  
then sinking,  
then swelling again,

like lungs.

Everything is being lifted  
and dirtied.  
Everything drinks  
from the same deep mouth.

The rain greens the field,  
fills the hoofprint,  
fattens the root,  
softens the grave.

And we go on calling it mercy,  
this bright exchange:  
what gives life  
also kills.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental poem about resonance: begin with deer running across a field, move to a musician thinking about a violin and prayer, then end in a garden with spring light and the heart’s ventricles. Make it lyrical, fragmented, and metaphysical.
counterfactuals.output:
Deer run across the field—  
not fleeing, exactly,  
but carrying the field forward  
in their brown, trembling bodies.

Grass breaks open beneath them.  
The air remembers hoofbeats  
as a bell remembers being struck.

And somewhere, a musician  
holds a violin without playing it,  
thinking: wood is a kind of listening.  
A hollow body,  
a chamber carved for longing.

He thinks of prayer—  
not words, not even silence,  
but the pressure before sound  
chooses a shape.

Bow above string.  
Breath above name.  
The invisible leans closer.

What is resonance  
but one solitude  
answering another?

The deer have vanished,  
yet the field still shivers.  
The violin rests in its case,  
yet the room hums faintly  
with a note no hand released.

In the garden, spring light  
arrives in fragments—  
gold on the spade,  
green fire in the shoots,  
the wet mouths of tulips  
opening toward nothing  
and everything.

Beneath the ribs,  
the heart’s ventricles  
fill and empty,  
fill and empty—

two dark rooms  
learning the bright law  
of return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a serious literary poem with no title, using long flowing lines and section breaks marked by “•”. Themes: perception, selfhood, trembling, music, February, spring brightness, the eternal return, and the paradox of life/death.
counterfactuals.output:
In February the light returns not as mercy but as an argument, a blade of brightness laid across the sill,  
and the room, which all winter had been thinking its one dark thought, begins to tremble with dust and music,  
each mote turning in the air as if perception were not sight but a kind of listening,  
as if the world could be heard entering itself again through the thawing pipes, the black branches,  
the small persistent rumor of water underneath the street’s bruised snow.

•

I have called myself by many names and none of them have answered except in passing,  
a face in glass, a shadow folded into another shadow, a pulse trying to remember its first astonishment;  
yet something in me goes on gathering the broken signatures of breath and gesture,  
making from them a self like a violin made from a tree that never entirely stops being a tree,  
its hollow body singing because it has been cut open, because emptiness was given a shape.

•

What is death but one name for the silence that listens beneath every note,  
and what is life but the brief trembling of the string above it, radiant with the wound of being struck?  
The blackbird on the wire does not solve this paradox, it spends it,  
flinging its dark syllables into the cold blue morning until the air itself seems mortal,  
and still the song returns, not the same song, never the same, but the same returning.

•

So the year circles back with its old newness, the crocus lifting its violet flame through the exhausted earth,  
spring brightness arriving as if it had not arrived countless times before,  
as if repetition were not a prison but the soul’s most ancient instrument,  
the eternal return of sap, thaw, wing, hunger, kiss, departure,  
each beginning carrying its grave within it, each ending secretly green at the root.

•

I stand at the window and cannot tell whether I am looking outward or being looked through,  
whether the trembling belongs to my hands, the branches, the music, or the light itself,  
for perception is a door that opens both ways and selfhood is the wind moving through it,  
unseen except by what it disturbs, known only by the shiver it leaves behind  
as February loosens its grip and the dead garden prepares, impossibly, to live again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic imitation of highbrow contemporary American verse: compressed syntax, rich sensory details, enjambed lines, and a reflective speaker linking animal motion, musical vibration, and blood circulation.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk the fox lifts  
from the ditch—red syllable,  
brushfire of muscle  
threading the frost-stiff weeds.

Under the porch, a cello  
leans into its darkened wood,  
one low string trembling  
as if the house itself  
had remembered water.

I stand there, wrist to throat,  
counting the small engine  
hidden in me: valves,  
their wet doors opening, shut,

opening—while overhead  
starlings write and erase  
one mind in the bruised air.

How close the body comes  
to music: hoofbeat, wing-burr,  
the bow’s black horsehair  
drawing from silence  
its vein of sound.

And the blood, obedient  
yet never still, goes on  
revising the red map—  
each pulse a footfall  
leaving no print,

each breath a note  
held briefly in the ribs  
before it vanishes, warm,  
into the listening dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
